content: Patient decision aids are tools specifically designed to assist individuals in making healthcare decisions. These aids explicitly outline the decision to be made, provide evidence-based information about the available options along with their associated benefits and risks, and help individuals clarify their personal values regarding the features of each option. This review is an update of a Cochrane review originally published in 2003 and last updated in 2017. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of patient decision aids on adults who are considering treatment or screening decisions. The review used an integrated knowledge translation approach. The updated search covered studies from 2015 to March 2022, including databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, EBSCO, and grey literature. The cumulative search spanned from the origins of these databases to March 2022. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared patient decision aids to usual care. Usual care was defined as general information, risk assessments, clinical practice guideline summaries for health consumers, placebo interventions (e.g., information on unrelated topics), or no intervention at all. Two authors independently screened studies for inclusion, extracted data on interventions and outcomes, and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. The primary outcomes were based on the International Patient Decision Aid Standards (IPDAS) and included attributes related to the choice made (such as congruence between informed values and care choices) and the decision-making process (such as knowledge, accurate risk perceptions, feeling informed, clarity of values, participation in decision-making, and adverse events). Secondary outcomes included the choice made, confidence in decision-making, adherence to the chosen option, preference-linked health outcomes, and the impact on the healthcare system (e.g., consultation length). The results were pooled using mean differences (MDs) and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), applying a random-effects model. A subgroup analysis compared studies included in the previous review (105 studies) to those published since the last update (104 studies). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. This updated review added 104 new studies, bringing the total to 209 studies involving 107,698 participants. The patient decision aids addressed 71 different healthcare decisions. The most common decisions were related to cardiovascular treatments (22 studies), cancer screening (17 studies on colorectal cancer, 15 on prostate cancer, 12 on breast cancer), cancer treatments (15 studies on breast cancer, 11 on prostate cancer), mental health treatments (10 studies), and joint replacement surgery (9 studies). When assessing the risk of bias, two items were frequently rated as unclear due to inadequate reporting: selective reporting (100 studies) and blinding of participants/personnel (161 studies). Of the 209 included studies, 34 had at least one item rated as high risk of bias. The review found moderate-certainty evidence that patient decision aids likely increase the congruence between informed values and care choices compared to usual care (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.13; 21 studies, 9377 participants). Regarding the decision-making process, there was high-certainty evidence that patient decision aids improve participants' knowledge (MD 11.90/100, 95% CI 10.60 to 13.19; 107 studies, 25,492 participants), enhance the accuracy of risk perceptions (RR 1.94, 95% CI 1.61 to 2.34; 25 studies, 7796 participants), and reduce decisional conflict related to feeling uninformed (MD -10.02, 95% CI -12.31 to -7.74; 58 studies, 12,104 participants) and indecision about personal values (MD -7.86, 95% CI -9.69 to -6.02; 55 studies, 11,880 participants). Additionally, the proportion of people who were passive in decision-making (clinician-controlled) decreased (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.88; 21 studies, 4348 participants). For adverse outcomes, there was high-certainty evidence that there was no difference in decision regret between the patient decision aid and usual care groups (MD -1.23, 95% CI -3.05 to 0.59; 22 studies, 3707 participants). The use of patient decision aids did not significantly affect the length of consultations when used in preparation for the consultation (MD -2.97 minutes, 95% CI -7.84 to 1.90; 5 studies, 420 participants). However, when patient decision aids were used during the consultation with the clinician, the consultation length increased by 1.5 minutes (MD 1.50 minutes, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.20; 8 studies, 2702 participants). The direction of the effects observed in studies included in the previous review was consistent with those observed in studies conducted since 2015. In conclusion, compared to usual care, patient decision aids likely help more adults make informed, values-congruent choices across a wide range of healthcare decisions. They significantly improve knowledge, the accuracy of risk perceptions, and active participation in decision-making. They also enhance patients' feelings of being informed and clear about their personal values. There was no difference in decision regret between individuals using decision aids and those receiving usual care. Further research is needed to evaluate the impact of patient decision aids on adherence to chosen options and their downstream effects on healthcare costs and resource utilization.
